# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

About the FT900...
Site Navigation:
MAIN | Statistics | Information | Services | Feedback | Site Index | Site Search
 

 

Foreign Trade Division FT900 Press Release files:

There is a legal mandate to publish foreign trade statistics. Title 13, Chapter 9 of the U.S. Code directs the Secretary of Commerce to collect, compile, and publish foreign trade statistics on a monthly and cumulative basis. The Bureau of the Census, Foreign Trade Division, is responsible for publishing the statistics.

The primary objective of the foreign trade statistical program is to produce the U.S. trade figures and other detailed import and export trade figures on a monthly basis. We must release this information on a pre-scheduled date each month, without exception.

We meet these requirements through the release of the highly publicized U.S. International Trade In Goods and Services report, commonly referred to as the FT900. The balance of trade figures, along with other various detailed foreign trade data, are released about 45 days after the statistical month covered.

The information under this menu provides the actual FT900 reports for the current month and year, as well as previous years. If you have questions or comments on this report, please contact the Data Dissemination Branch.

Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: US International Trade in Goods and Services
Description: The U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services program is a monthly release providing comprehensive data on U.S. trade balance, exports, and imports. It covers physical goods and services, measuring international transactions.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research this dataset comprehensively. The title suggests this is the joint Census Bureau/BEA "FT-900" monthly trade release. Let me verify and gather details.I've confirmed the FT-900 joint release and its legal mandate. Now I'll dig deeper into BEA's authority, the historical origins, data sources, and how the data is used.Now let me get details on typical users/uses and access/distribution channels (API, USA Trade Online, FRED), plus the market sensitivity/embargo aspects.I have most of the picture. Let me get one more round: the "About the FT900" page (uses/production process) and preservation-related details (historical series, data products, API/USA Trade Online).# Research Report: U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services (FT-900)

## Executive Summary

The dataset described is the **FT-900: U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services**, a monthly statistical release published jointly by the **U.S. Census Bureau** (Foreign Trade Division, within the Department of Commerce) and the **U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA)**. The user's description is accurate: it is a monthly release providing the official U.S. trade balance (deficit/surplus) along with detailed exports and imports of both goods and services. It is one of the most closely watched principal federal economic indicators, released on a fixed schedule at 8:30 a.m. Eastern time, embargoed until release, and free to the public.

---

## 1. Publisher and Institutional Roles

- **U.S. Census Bureau, Foreign Trade Division (FTD)** — responsible for collecting, compiling, and publishing the goods trade statistics (roughly 9,000 export commodity codes and 18,000 import commodity codes).
- **U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA)** — collects and compiles the services trade statistics via mandatory surveys and produces the balance-of-payments (BOP) basis figures.
- Each release carries joint release numbers (e.g., "CB 26-160, BEA 26-44") and is posted simultaneously at **census.gov/ft900** and **bea.gov/data/intl-trade-investment/international-trade-goods-and-services**.

This joint structure matters for data librarians: there are effectively two "homes" for the data, and some historical material exists on one site but not the other.

## 2. Legal Authority and Mandate

The program rests on multiple statutes — this is one of the few economic statistics programs with an explicit legal mandate to publish on a pre-scheduled monthly basis, "without exception":

**For goods (Census Bureau):**
- **Title 13, U.S. Code, Chapter 9 (13 U.S.C. § 301 et seq.)** — directs the Secretary of Commerce to collect, compile, and publish foreign trade statistics monthly and cumulatively.
- **18 U.S.C. § 1905** — protects the confidentiality of business information.
- **15 CFR Part 30 (§§ 30.90–30.91)** — the regulatory mandate governing export reporting (the Foreign Trade Regulations), implemented through the Automated Export System (AES).

**For services (BEA):**
- **The International Investment and Trade in Services Survey Act (P.L. 94-472; 22 U.S.C. §§ 3101–3108)** — mandatory reporting authority for BEA's services surveys (e.g., quarterly BE-180-type surveys and the benchmark BE-120 survey conducted every five years), implemented via **15 CFR Part 801**.
- **The Omnibus Trade and Competitiveness Act of 1988 (15 U.S.C. § 4908)** — additional authority for financial services surveys and, notably, the requirement that led to the constant/real dollar series.

**Confidentiality provisions:** Data are collected for statistical purposes only. BEA's survey data cannot be used for tax, regulatory, or investigative purposes and are exempt from FOIA under 22 U.S.C. § 3104(c).

## 3. History

The FT-900 has one of the longest lineages of any federal statistical product:

- **1790–1820:** Annual import/export statements compiled by the Treasury Department from customs collectors' reports and transmitted to Congress (published in the *American State Papers*).
- **1820:** Act of Congress (Feb. 10, 1820) required statistical accounts of foreign commerce showing kinds, quantities, and values of articles by country; annual publication in *Commerce and Navigation of the United States* began in 1821.
- **1866:** Treasury's Bureau of Statistics established.
- **1903:** Trade statistics function transferred to the new Department of Commerce and Labor.
- **1941:** The Division of Foreign Trade Statistics was moved into the U.S. Census Bureau — its institutional home ever since.
- **1987:** U.S.–Canada Memorandum of Understanding creating the data exchange: U.S. exports to Canada are compiled from Canadian import statistics (and vice versa), an arrangement still in effect.
- **January 1989:** Commodities reclassified under the Harmonized Tariff Schedule (HTS).
- **January 1990:** First publication of seasonally adjusted constant-dollar (inflation-adjusted) trade data, per the 1988 Omnibus Trade Act.
- **January 1994:** **The FT-900 as we know it began** — Census (goods) and BEA (services) combined forces and began issuing the joint monthly press release *U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services*.
- **2003:** Constant-dollar series replaced with chain-weighted (real) dollars for consistency with other Commerce statistics (with the April 2003 data).
- **2010:** New methodology for estimating low-value (below-reporting-threshold) shipments, including a courier-shipment factor.
- **2015–present era:** The Census **Advance Economic Indicators Report** now provides advance goods-trade figures ~24–26 days after the reference month; the FT-900 follows ~34–36 days after (historically ~45 days) with complete coverage, full commodity/country detail, BOP-basis goods data, and services.

Historical time series extend back to **1960 (annual)** and **1992 (monthly)** on the Census historical data pages.

## 4. Data Sources and Methodology

- **Goods exports:** Electronic Export Information (EEI) filed by the U.S. Principal Party in Interest (USPPI) or agents through the Automated Export System (AES) — administrative data, not a survey. Exports to Canada come from the Canadian import data exchange.
- **Goods imports:** Data filed with U.S. Customs and Border Protection, chiefly through the Automated Commercial Environment (ACE) and entry summary/warehouse/foreign trade zone documents; electricity and natural gas imports from Canada come from Canadian sources.
- **Services:** BEA estimates from quarterly, annual, and benchmark (every five years) mandatory surveys of U.S. and foreign persons; no country detail for services due to source-data limits. Services cover transactions between foreign countries and the 50 states, D.C., Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, and other territories; U.S. military/diplomatic installations abroad are excluded as part of the U.S. economy.
- **Valuation/basis:** Goods figures are published both on a **Census basis** (customs-type definitions) and **BOP basis** (adjusted to balance-of-payments concepts); the headline deficit is on the BOP basis.
- **Revision policy:** Prior month revised each release; quarterly revisions to chain-weighted dollars; **annual revisions each June** redistribute late-arriving transactions to the correct month, apply corrections, and recompile the prior three years (plus seasonal factor re-estimation).

Because these are administrative records rather than sample surveys, sampling error is not applicable — the release explicitly notes "statistical significance is not applicable or not measurable."

## 5. Content and Structure

The FT-900 comprises ~20 exhibits plus supplements: total trade, three-month moving averages, services detail, goods by principal end-use category (foods/feeds, capital goods, automotive, consumer goods, industrial supplies), real (chain-weighted) dollars, non-seasonally adjusted data, trade by selected countries and areas, SITC commodity detail, Advanced Technology Products (ATP), petroleum/energy products, crude oil by country, motor vehicles and parts by country, NAICS-based product categories, and **exports by state**. Files are distributed as PDF (~1.5 MB) and a ZIP of XLSX exhibits (~7 MB).

## 6. Access and Distribution Channels

- Current release: **census.gov/ft900** and the BEA newsroom.
- Historical releases: Census FT-900 historical archive (back to the late 1990s online) — note Census's caveat that historical releases are *not* further revised; revised data live in the historical time-series files (annual from 1960, monthly from 1992).
- **USA Trade Online** (usatradeonline.census.gov): interactive tool for detailed commodity/country queries.
- **International Trade API** with an API Query Builder tool (machine-readable access for data scientists).
- Census Economic Briefing Room and scheduled release calendar; BEA release schedule.
- Widely mirrored by secondary sources (FRED, news services, commercial data vendors).

## 7. Typical Users and Uses

- **Macroeconomic policymakers:** The FT-900 is the primary source for goods trade data in BEA's quarterly **GDP** estimates and the U.S. balance of payments; the Federal Reserve monitors it for inflation, demand, and growth signals (net trade directly affects GDP arithmetic).
- **Financial markets:** A market-moving, embargoed release at 8:30 a.m. ET; deficits exceeding expectations move bond, currency, and equity markets, and shape interest-rate expectations.
- **Trade policymakers:** Country- and commodity-level detail underpins tariff analysis, trade negotiations, enforcement (antidumping/countervailing duty cases), export controls, and Section 232/301-type proceedings.
- **Businesses:** Exporters and importers track the global marketplace for their products, identify new markets, and benchmark market share (Census explicitly cites this purpose).
- **Researchers, journalists, and the public:** The trade deficit is among the most politically salient economic statistics, routinely headline news each month.

## 8. Public Benefits

1. **Constitutionally rooted transparency** — a continuous public record of U.S. commerce since 1790, published free, in machine-readable form, on a legally mandated fixed schedule.
2. **Foundation of the national accounts** — indispensable to GDP and international accounts.
3. **Evidence base for policy debate** — lets the public, advocates, and Congress evaluate trade agreements, tariffs, and industrial policy with authoritative data.
4. **Business intelligence** — helps small and large firms find export markets, at no cost.
5. **Confidentiality safeguards** — mandatory reporting is paired with strict statistical-use-only protections, sustaining private-sector cooperation and data integrity.

## 9. Notes for Preservationists and Data Librarians

- The FT-900 exists as **fixed press-release snapshots** (never revised after posting) versus a **living revised historical series** — a critical distinction when archiving; cite the release date as part of the identifier (e.g., "FT-900, August 2026, released October 6, 2026, CB 26-160 / BEA 26-44").
- Older releases exist in PDF (and earlier formats) on Census's FT-900 index; the exhibit history covers 1992–present; annual revisions are separately posted.
- The dual Census/BEA publication means both agencies' sites should be captured for a complete archive; URL patterns have changed multiple times over the decades (legacy `www2.census.gov` pages still host older documentation, some dating to 1999).

## Verification of the User's Description

The user's title and description are **accurate and verified**, with two refinements worth noting: (1) the standard short name is "U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services," commonly referred to as the **FT-900**, published jointly by the Census Bureau and BEA; and (2) while goods data are drawn from customs/administrative records, the services data are survey-based estimates compiled by BEA — so "covers physical goods and services" is correct, but the two components are produced through entirely different collection regimes.

I'll research current risks to this dataset: recent news on the Census Bureau and BEA, budget and staffing changes, the 2025 government shutdown's effect on trade data releases, and any policy proposals affecting trade statistics.I have solid evidence on the shutdown delays, budget proposals, and the proposed agency reorganization. Now let me research policy proposals specific to trade-deficit calculation changes, data removals from agency websites, the staffing tracker, and the current (2026) status of the reorganization.# Risk Assessment: U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services (FT-900)

**Assessment date:** October 2026. Publishers: U.S. Census Bureau (Foreign Trade Division) and Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), both within the Department of Commerce.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence:**
- The Census FT-900 historical index (census.gov/foreign-trade/Press-Release/ft900_index.html) currently lists complete monthly releases (PDF + XLSX ZIP ~6.9 MB each) and annual revisions back through the release history, including the shutdown-affected months (September–December 2025, Annual Revisions 2025, January–February 2026), all accessible.
- Historical time series (annual from 1960, monthly from 1992) remain posted on Census's foreign-trade pages; USA Trade Online and the International Trade API remain operational.
- However, the broader environment shows removals at the same agencies: BEA publicly announced discontinuation of multiple datasets in 2024–2025 (multinational-enterprise statistics in July and November 2025, several FDI and NIPA tables, the Digital Economy Satellite Account, Integrated Macroeconomic Accounts), and the Senate Appropriations Committee's FY2026 report explicitly directed Census to account for "the removal of Census and BEA data sets." A community "Federal Data Terminations Tracker" (essentialdata.us) documents removals agency-wide.
- No evidence of any removal or alteration of FT-900 historical releases or the underlying trade time series specifically. Notably, trade statistics are the *one* program the FY2026 BEA budget explicitly commits to prioritize as "mandated by law... the U.S. trade balance."

**Risk level: No Known Issue** — for this dataset, all historical files remain publicly available and unaltered. (Agency-wide removal trends at BEA/Census warrant continued monitoring, but they have hit supplementary products, not the FT-900.)

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence:**
- The 43-day government shutdown (Oct 1–Nov 12, 2025) suspended collection and publication. The FT-900 for August 2025 (due Oct 7) was released Nov 19, 2025; September 2025 (due Nov 4) released Dec 11; October 2025 (due Dec 4) released Jan 8, 2026; November 2025 released Jan 29, 2026 (Census GovDelivery bulletin 10/2025; BEA schedule-update blogs 11/14, 11/24, 12/4, 12/19/2025). No monthly observation was ultimately skipped — all months were eventually published.
- Recovery is complete: the release schedule normalized in 2026, with e.g. the August 2026 report released October 6, 2026 (CB 26-160 / BEA 26-44) and the June 2026 annual revision cycle completed on time.
- ICRs remain active: BEA's mandatory services surveys (the collection instrument for the services component) were the subject of routine Federal Register renewal notice in January 2026 (FR 2026-00691) — no lapse.
- The statutory monthly mandate (13 U.S.C. ch. 9) was not formally waived, but intended publication dates were missed for four consecutive cycles in 2025–26.

**Risk level: Moderate Risk** — intended publication dates were missed and collection/publication delayed by the funding lapse, but publication resumed on schedule, no cycle was skipped, and ICRs are active. (Not High Risk: no terminated collection, and the delays were shutdown-driven rather than programmatic.)

---

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence:**
- Granularity, frequency, and content of the FT-900 itself are unchanged: the same ~20 exhibits (country detail, end-use categories, SITC/NAICS detail, ATP, state exports, real dollars, services detail) continue to be published; the report now explicitly describes a 34–36 day release lag (vs. the historical ~45 days), an improvement in timeliness.
- Temporary timeliness degradation occurred during the shutdown backlog (releases running ~2 months late at the peak), now resolved.
- Emerging risks: BEA has lost ~20% of staff since FY2024 (ASA, "The Nation's Data at Risk 2025") including a 76-FTE program reduction in its National/Regional/International Economic Accounts; BEA has publicly said it is "focusing resources on mandated statistics and away from supplementary estimates" and "streamlining other datasets." BEA also disclosed it could no longer purchase IRS Statistics of Income data for the 2025 annual update of other accounts — evidence of resource-driven quality trade-offs at the agency, though not (yet) touching trade data.
- The trade data's methodology (administrative AES/ACE records for goods; mandatory surveys for services) is unaffected by the response-rate pressures plaguing household surveys.

**Risk level: Moderate Risk** — no realized reduction in the FT-900's granularity or frequency, but staff and budget losses at BEA/Census create genuine, documented emerging risk to timeliness and detail, and a temporary timeliness reduction already occurred in 2025.

---

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence:**
- Title 13 U.S.C. Chapter 9 explicitly directs monthly collection, compilation, and publication of foreign trade statistics; Census regulations (15 CFR Part 30) and the AES mandate implement it. Services are covered by the International Investment and Trade in Services Survey Act (22 U.S.C. §§ 3101–3108; 15 CFR Part 801).
- The FY2026 BEA budget submission itself names "the U.S. trade balance" among statistics "mandated by law" it will prioritize — the administration's own documents concede this program cannot be dropped.
- No substitute exists: customs entries and AES filings have no alternative public collection; the FT-900 is the primary source for goods trade in BEA's GDP and the international accounts (the release says so explicitly), making it required for implementation of federal programs (national accounts, tariff/trade policy, antidumping enforcement).

**Risk level: No Known Issue** — explicit statutory mandate, unambiguous specification of what must be collected, no alternative data source, and essential to federal program implementation. This is among the most legally protected datasets in the federal statistical system.

---

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence:**
- **Census Bureau:** lost an estimated 15% of staff since FY2024 (ASA); Rep. Meng (House CJS hearing, June 2025) cited "the loss of over 1,000 Census Bureau staff" — meeting the rubric's "1,000 or more staff lost" threshold. DOGE terminated five reimbursable surveys in May 2025; DOGE/deferred-resignation and RIF planning under the February 11, 2025 executive order continued through 2025.
- **BEA:** ~20% staffing loss since FY2024; FY2026 request of $111M vs. FY2025's $117.3M (an ~8% cut in purchasing power, per ASA).
- However, the trade program specifically was level-funded: the FY2026 request for Current Economic Statistics (which includes foreign trade at Census) was $216M, flat with FY2024/FY2025 actuals, and the enacted FY2026 CJS bill (P.L. 119-74) funded Census at $1.490B (an increase overall, with Current Surveys at $319M, down only ~$10M/3%).
- Leadership: Commerce Secretary Lutnick fired the BLS commissioner (a different bureau) in August 2025 and told statistical staff that independence is "nonsense"; Census advisory committees and FESAC were disbanded (Feb–Mar 2025). The fate of the proposed statistical-agency reorganization (see Policy) leaves the leadership structure unsettled.

**Risk level: High Risk** — the rubric's threshold is met at the producing-agency level (1,000+ staff lost at Census; 20% at BEA; budget cuts in purchasing power; leadership turmoil across Commerce statistical agencies). Important nuance: none of the documented cuts have directly hit the foreign-trade program's funding line, and the trade balance is explicitly prioritized as mandated.

---

## 6. Policy

**Evidence:**
- **Pending reorganization:** The FY2026 President's Budget proposes to "reorganize the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Bureau of Economic Analysis, and the Census Bureau at the Department of Commerce"; Lutnick confirmed to Congress in June 2025 that this merger (echoing Project 2025) is the plan, but details, timeline, and legislative status remain unspecified as of the latest available reporting. This directly involves *both* publishers of the FT-900.
- **Realized changes at the same agencies:** DOGE survey terminations without public-comment process (May 2025); disbanding of FESAC and Census advisory committees (Feb–Mar 2025); firing of the BLS commissioner after an unfavorable jobs report; Lutnick's "independence is nonsense" remarks — a pattern that statistical-community groups (ASA, CBPP, Census Project) describe as political pressure on federal statistics.
- **Dataset-specific exposure is low:** no negative policy note on the FT-900 pages; no ICR disruption; no tariff-driven effort documented to change the deficit methodology (the administration's tariff regime *consumes* FT-900 country/commodity detail rather than suppressing it). BEA's budget submission protects the trade balance as core.
- Congressional pushback exists: Senate CJS report directing Census to explain data removals and the enacted FY2026 bill partially restoring funding.

**Risk level: Moderate Risk** — significant realized changes at the parent agencies (terminations, disbandings, dismissals) and a pending merger of both publishers, but no administration action targeting the FT-900's collection or publication; if anything, the administration relies on this data for its trade agenda. (The realized DOGE terminations at Census keep this category close to the High Risk boundary; the fact that they hit reimbursable surveys rather than statutorily mandated trade statistics is what holds it at Moderate.)

---

## Summary of Risk Levels

**Historical Data Availability: No Known Issue** — all FT-900 historical releases and series remain fully accessible, though removals have occurred to *other* BEA/Census datasets.

**Future Data Availability: Moderate Risk** — publication dates were missed for four cycles (Oct 2025–Jan 2026) due to the shutdown; fully recovered and on schedule in 2026, with ICRs active.

**Data Quality: Moderate Risk** — granularity and frequency maintained (and release lag improved to 34–36 days), but staffing losses (~20% at BEA, 15%/1,000+ at Census) and BEA's shift away from "supplementary estimates" create documented emerging risk.

**Statutory Context: No Known Issue** — explicit statutory mandate (13 U.S.C. ch. 9; 22 U.S.C. §§ 3101–3108), no substitute data collection, and essential to GDP and trade-policy implementation.

**Staffing and Funding: High Risk** — 1,000+ staff lost at Census and ~20% at BEA since FY2024 meet the rubric's High Risk threshold, even though the trade program's own funding line was held flat and the program is protected as mandated.

**Policy: Moderate Risk** — pending proposal to merge/consolidate both publishing agencies, plus realized terminations and advisory-committee disbandments agency-wide, but no policy action aimed at the FT-900, which the administration actively uses for its tariff agenda.

**Overall assessment:** The FT-900 sits in an unusual position — it is one of the most legally protected and administratively indispensable datasets in the federal statistical system (mandated by statute, feeding GDP, and central to the administration's own trade policy), yet it is produced by two agencies undergoing severe staffing losses, budget pressure, and a pending structural merger. The most plausible near-term risks are not deletion of the dataset but *indirect*: shutdown-driven release delays (already realized once), degraded timeliness or detail if staff losses deepen, and disruption during any Census/BEA reorganization. Preservationists should prioritize capturing the pre-merger state of both agencies' websites and the historical release archive now, while the data itself remains intact and freely available.
